procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated April 13, 1966 of the Madras High Court in Writ Petitions Nos. 390 of 1965 etc.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed two writ petitions before the High Court: one for a writ of mandamus directing the forbearing from prosecution of C.C. No. 10 of 1964 and a second for a writ of certiorari to quash the order of the Special Judge. There was also a petition under ss. 435/439 of the Criminal Procedure Code for revision of the order of the Special Judge and one under s. 561-A of the Code for quashing his said order. The High Court dealt with all the Writ Petitions and the different allied matters together.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court after the High Court issued its judgment and order. The appeals arise out of certificates granted by the High Court of Madras arising out of two Writ Petitions and a petition under ss. 435 and 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure filed in that court by P. Sirajuddin.

directions: The Special Judge will follow the directions of the High Court in addition to the modification indicated by us.

issue.issue_text: Whether the investigation commenced on 15th April 1964, when the Director of Vigilance registered an inquiry, or only after the formal first information report was lodged on June 27, 1964.

facts: The Director of Vigilance registered an inquiry on April 15, 1964.
The Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption only became a designated "police station" for the purposes of the Criminal Procedure Code through a notification dated May 25, 1964.
A formal first information report was lodged on June 27, 1964.
law: An investigation under Chapter XIV of the Code of Criminal Procedure is one conducted by a police station.
application: The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's finding on this point.

The Court reasoned that since the Directorate of Vigilance was not legally a "police station" until May 25, 1964, the inquiry it conducted before that date (starting on April 15) could not be considered a formal investigation under the Code.
Therefore, the inquiry prior to the Directorate becoming a police station was a preliminary inquiry, not a statutory investigation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that, technically, the investigation under the Code of Criminal Procedure did not commence on April 15, 1964. It only started after the formal first information report was lodged on June 27, 1964, because the investigating body did not have the legal status of a police station until May 25, 1964.

issue.issue_text: Whether the taking of signed and self-incriminating statements from witnesses during the inquiry was in violation of sections 161 to 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, causing prejudice to the appellant.

facts: During an inquiry conducted before a formal First Information Report (FIR) was lodged, an investigating officer recorded self-incriminating statements from several witnesses.
The officer had these witnesses sign their statements.
The officer also gave 'certificates of immunity' to at least two witnesses, promising them protection from prosecution for their own roles in the matter.
The State argued that the procedural rules of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) did not apply because these actions took place before a formal FIR was registered.
law: Chapter XIV of the Code of Criminal Procedure is designed to ensure a fair investigation.
Section 162(1) of the Cr.P.C. explicitly prohibits a police officer from having a witness sign a statement that has been reduced to writing during the course of an investigation.

Statements recorded after receiving definite information about the commission of an offense are considered part of the 'investigation' and are subject to Section 162, even if the formal registration of an FIR is delayed.
Statements obtained through inducement, threat, or promise (such as an offer of immunity) are improper, as per Section 24 of the Indian Evidence Act.
application: The Supreme Court strongly condemned the investigating officer's methods, stating he 'deliberately overstepped the limits of investigation'.
The Court found that taking signed statements was a direct violation of Section 162 of the Cr.P.C., done with the obvious intent of 'pinning them down' to their testimony.

It rejected the State's argument that the rules did not apply before the FIR was lodged. The Court held that as soon as the officer had information suggesting the appellant's guilt, he was obligated to lodge an FIR and follow the proper legal procedure.

The Court concluded that the 'certificates of immunity' were an inducement, and it was unbelievable that the self-incriminating statements were made before at least an oral assurance of immunity was given.

This entire course of investigation was deemed 'grossly irregular and unfair' and could not be excused by claiming proper procedure was followed after the FIR was eventually filed. The Court held that this failure to follow the law from the outset caused prejudice to the appellant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appellant's argument, concluding that the taking of signed and self-incriminating statements, particularly through the inducement of immunity, was a clear violation of sections 161 to 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court held that this illegal and unfair investigation method caused prejudice to the appellant and affirmed the High Court's direction to exclude these tainted statements from consideration.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Special Judge erred in framing a charge without excluding the illegally obtained statements, and whether the matter should be reconsidered after excluding such evidence.

facts: An investigating officer conducted an inquiry where he recorded signed, self-incriminating statements from various witnesses.
Some of these witnesses were given assurances of immunity from prosecution.
The appellant argued that this process violated sections 161 to 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code, making the statements illegal.
The Special Judge considered these statements and framed a charge against the appellant.
The appellant challenged this decision, and the High Court ruled in his favor, ordering the Special Judge to reconsider the case after excluding the tainted statements.
law: Statements recorded during an investigation that are signed, self-incriminating, or confessional in nature, especially when obtained through inducement or promise, are considered illegal as they violate the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code (specifically ss. 161-164).
application: The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court that "serious irregularities were committed" during the investigation which were prejudicial to the appellant.
The Court found that the investigator's actions, such as taking signed, self-incriminating statements and offering immunity, were improper and violated established legal procedures.
It concluded that the Special Judge was wrong to rely on this illegally obtained evidence when deciding to frame the charge.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court affirmed the High Court's decision. It held that the Special Judge had erred in framing the charge without first excluding the illegally obtained statements. The Court upheld the direction for the Special Judge to reconsider the matter and decide whether to frame a charge only after excluding the tainted evidence from consideration.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the investigation commenced on 15th April 1964, when the Director of Vigilance registered an inquiry, or only after the formal first information report was lodged on June 27, 1964.
appellant_arguments: The investigation commenced on the earlier date (April 15, 1964) when the inquiry was registered, meaning the statements taken thereafter were part of a formal investigation governed by the Code of Criminal Procedure.
respondent_arguments: The formal investigation under Chapter XIV of the Code of Criminal Procedure only began on the later date (June 27, 1964) when the first information report was lodged.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the taking of signed and self-incriminating statements from witnesses during the inquiry was in violation of sections 161 to 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, causing prejudice to the appellant.
appellant_arguments: The investigation was conducted improperly, with an attempt to lay a guideline for prosecution witnesses.
Signed, confessional, and self-incriminating statements were taken from numerous witnesses who had been given assurances of immunity, which prejudiced the appellant's case.
respondent_arguments: Assurances of immunity were given to only two persons, and only after they had already provided their signed statements.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Special Judge erred in framing a charge without excluding the illegally obtained statements, and whether the matter should be reconsidered after excluding such evidence.
appellant_arguments: The charge framed by the Special Judge was groundless as it relied on illegally obtained evidence, and therefore the proceedings should be quashed or reconsidered without that evidence.
respondent_arguments: The charge was validly framed by the Special Judge based on the evidence presented.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A person who is the head of a department and actively responsible for directing the commission of offenses by subordinates cannot be allowed to take the plea that the case against them should not proceed unless the subordinates are also joined as co-accused.
obiter: The evidence of a witness who had previously signed a statement in writing does not become inadmissible or vitiate the whole proceeding, although the value of the evidence would be seriously impaired thereby.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the procedure adopted by the state during the preliminary inquiry, before the first information report was lodged, was grossly improper and prejudicial to the appellant. While a preliminary inquiry is permissible, the investigators' failure to file an FIR as soon as it became clear the appellant appeared guilty, and their subsequent actions of obtaining signed, self-incriminating statements from numerous witnesses under assurances of immunity, was an unprecedented and outrageous procedure that violated the principles of justice and fair play.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the pre-investigation procedure, though not explicitly forbidden by law, is so outrageous as to violate fundamental principles of justice and fair play.

The requirement under Chapter XIV of the Code of Criminal Procedure that once a preliminary inquiry reveals a prima facie case of serious misconduct, a formal first information report must be lodged to commence a proper investigation.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that he was unfairly singled out for prosecution while his subordinates were not was rejected. The court reasoned that if the appellant, as the head of the department, was actively responsible for directing his subordinates to commit offenses, he cannot demand that they be joined as co-accused as a condition for his own prosecution.
why_respondent_won: The respondent (the State) successfully argued that the prosecution has the discretion to not charge subordinate officers, particularly if they were acting under the appellant's direction and their evidence was necessary for the case. The court held that the appellant, as the alleged main perpetrator, could not use the non-prosecution of his subordinates as a shield.
policy_considerations: While the State has a duty to track down and punish delinquent officers, their conviction cannot be sought through questionable means that violate justice and fair play.
A preliminary inquiry into allegations against a high-ranking public servant is a proper course of action to avoid the incalculable harm of a baseless public charge.

However, once a preliminary inquiry reveals that an officer appears to be guilty of serious misconduct, it is the duty of the investigating agency to lodge a formal first information report and proceed with the investigation according to the rules of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The practice of obtaining signed, confessional, and self-incriminatory statements from potential witnesses by assuring them of immunity is highly irregular and amounts to an improper attempt to lay a guideline for their future testimony at trial.
